Trees

Trees organise data as a hierarchy, from one root down to many leaves. This page covers the vocabulary and the recursive pattern behind almost every tree problem, four traversal orders, binary search trees with insert, search and delete, why balance matters, heaps stored in arrays, and tries for words.

Part 1

🌲What a tree is

A tree stores items in a hierarchy. One node at the top is the root. Every other node has exactly one parent, and any node can have children below it. A node with no children is a leaf. Folders on a computer, the parts of a web page and a company org chart are all trees.

WordMeaningIn the tree below
rootthe only node with no parent1
childrennodes directly below a node2 and 3 are children of 1
leafa node with no children4, 5 and 6
depthedges from the root down to a nodedepth of 5 is 2
heightnumber of levels in the tree3
subtreea node together with everything below it2, 4, 5

In a binary tree every node has at most two children, called left and right. Each node is an object holding a value and two references, just like a linked list node with two next pointers.

Most tree code follows one pattern: handle the empty tree, solve the left subtree, solve the right subtree, then combine the two answers with the current node.

🔢 Edges

Every node except the root hangs from exactly one edge, so a tree with n nodes always has n − 1 edges.

edges = n − 1

📏 Levels

Level d of a binary tree holds at most 2d nodes, so a tree with h full levels holds at most 2h − 1 nodes.

n ≤ 2h − 1
Part 2

🚶Traversals: visiting every node

A traversal visits every node once. Depth first traversals go deep before going wide, and differ only in when the node itself is visited compared with its two subtrees.

OrderRuleResult for the treeTypical use
Preordernode, left, right1 2 4 5 3 6copying or saving a tree
Inorderleft, node, right4 2 5 1 3 6sorted output from a search tree
Postorderleft, right, node4 5 2 6 3 1deleting a tree, folder sizes
Level orderrow by row with a queue1 2 3 4 5 6shortest number of steps, printing by level

Level order cannot use recursion directly, because it jumps between branches. A queue keeps the nodes waiting in the order they were found, which is breadth first search on a tree.

Every traversal takes O(n) time. Recursion uses O(h) memory for the call stack, where h is the height. Level order uses memory for the widest level.
Part 3

🔍Binary search trees

A binary search tree (BST) adds one rule: everything in the left subtree of a node is smaller than the node, and everything in the right subtree is larger. That rule turns every node into a signpost. To find a value, compare and go left or right, throwing away a whole subtree at every step.

OperationBalanced treeWorst case (a chain)
searchO(log n)O(n)
insertO(log n)O(n)
deleteO(log n)O(n)
sorted listingO(n)O(n)
minimum or maximumO(log n)O(n)
Inorder traversal of a BST always produces the values in sorted order. Exams love asking for it, and it is also the quickest way to check that a tree really is a BST.
Part 4

✂️Deleting from a search tree

Deleting is the only tricky BST operation, because the tree must keep its ordering rule. First find the node, then handle one of three cases.

🍃 A leaf

Just remove it. Its parent now points to nothing.

☝️ One child

Lift the child into the node's place. Everything in that subtree is still on the correct side of the parent.

✌️ Two children

Find the inorder successor: the smallest value in the right subtree, found by going right once and then left as far as possible. Copy that value into the node, then delete the successor from the right subtree. The successor has no left child, so that second delete is always one of the easy cases.

The inorder predecessor (the largest value in the left subtree) works just as well. Both are the closest values to the one being removed, so the order is kept.
Part 5

⚖️Balance: why shape matters

A BST is only fast when it is short. Insert values that are already sorted and every new node becomes a right child, so the tree turns into a chain that is no better than a linked list.

The shortest possible binary tree with n nodes has this height:

h = ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉

For a million nodes that is only 20 levels, so a search needs at most 20 comparisons. A chain of a million nodes might need a million.

Self balancing treeIdeaUsed in
AVL treeheights of the two subtrees differ by at most 1, fixed with rotationslookup heavy in memory indexes
Red black treecolour rules keep the longest path at most twice the shortestJava TreeMap, C++ std::map
B treemany keys per node, all leaves on one leveldatabases and file systems
Python and JavaScript have no built in balanced search tree. For sorted keys in Python, the bisect module on a sorted list or the third party sortedcontainers package is the usual answer.
Part 6

⛰️Heaps: trees inside arrays

A binary heap is a complete binary tree: every level is full except possibly the last, which fills from the left. In a min heap every parent is smaller than or equal to its children, so the smallest value is always at the root.

Because the tree is complete, it fits in a plain array with no references at all. The node at index i finds its family with arithmetic:

left = 2i + 1   right = 2i + 2   parent = ⌊(i − 1) / 2⌋
HeapBinary search tree
Smallest valueO(1) peekO(log n)
InsertO(log n)O(log n) when balanced
Search any valueO(n)O(log n) when balanced
Storageone arraynodes and references
Python has heapq, Java has PriorityQueue. Heaps power priority queues, heap sort, Dijkstra's shortest paths and finding the top k items.
Part 7

🔤Tries: trees of letters

A trie (also called a prefix tree) stores words letter by letter. Each edge is one letter, and words that share a beginning share the same path. A flag on a node marks where a complete word ends.

⚡ Speed

Searching a word of length L takes O(L) steps, whether the trie holds ten words or ten million.

⌨️ Autocomplete

Walk down the typed prefix, then collect every word below that node. Phone keyboards and search boxes do exactly this.

Choose a trie when the questions are about prefixes. Choose a hash set when you only ever ask whether a whole word exists.
